body.text: Interest rates live updates: RBA expected to hike cash rate to 18-year high of 4.85 per cent
The Reserve Bank's interest rate setting board is today widely expected to lift the cash rate to an 18-year high of 4.85 per cent.
It follows senior central bank officials warning inflation was still too high, which fuelled the expectations of a fifth hike this year.
Follow the day's financial news and insights from our specialist business reporters on our live blog.
Disclaimer: this blog is not intended as investment advice.
Submit a comment or question
Live updates
RBA interest rate decision at 2:30pm AEDT
Welcome to our live coverage of the Reserve Bank's November meeting.
The RBA's Monetary Policy Board will announce its interest rate decision at 2:30pm AEDT.
Expectations are for the cash rate to be raised for a fifth time this year, taking it to 4.85%.
At the same time, the central bank will release updated economic forecasts in its quarterly Statement on Monetary Policy.
This will be followed by a press conference with RBA governor Michele Bullock at 3:30pm.
We will have full coverage, market reaction and analysis here on the blog, so stick with us.
And please drop us a comment in the meantime.

Future of David Jones in spotlight ahead of Christmas
Iconic department store David Jones is being forced to defend its future viability, as the Australian retailer faces speculation about store closures and misses a crucial filing deadline.
The department store's key lender has already chipped in extra cash before Christmas to allow David Jones to stock up for the busy festive season.
Hilco Capital wouldn't confirm the figure, but the ABC understands it to be about $10 million.
You can read more about it from reporter Emilia Terzon here.
CBA revises home prices forecast
Whatever the opposite is of a sigh of relief (perhaps a collective groan?)... well, I can hear that from homeowners across the country.

Yesterday, it was all about the dismal data from Cotality - now, it's CBA bringing a plate to the pity party. The bank has updated it's forecast saying home prices are to record the largest downturn on record.
Here are some of their sobering predictions:

■ We have revised down our dwelling price forecasts again. We now expect national dwelling prices to fall by around 14% from peak to trough this cycle, while the five‑capital city average is expected to trough around 15% below its most recent peak.
■ The downgrade reflects a faster and broader correction than expected at our last update on 1 September.

■ We expect materially deeper falls in Brisbane and Perth, with 18% peak‑to‑trough falls in both cities as fading overexuberance takes hold and more than offsets the effect of tight supply conditions. We also now expect peak‑to‑trough falls of around 16% in Sydney and 13% in Melbourne and Adelaide.■ National dwelling prices are now forecast to fall by 8% over 2026 and a further 3% over 2027. We expect prices to stabilise during the second half of 2027, supported in part by our expectation that the RBA begins cutting rates late next year following a further 25bp hike to 4.85% in November.The downturn has been faster and broader than expected.
This, of course, just two hours from the RBA's rates decision with markets largely pricing in a 25 basis point hike. ("AGAIN?!", I hear you say). CBA predicts the same - this is their forecast:

We expect the RBA to raise the cash rate by a further 25bp to 4.85% at its November meeting later today, before remaining on hold until 25bp cuts in August and November 2027. This is higher than the profile underpinning our September dwelling price forecasts, which assumed the cash rate would peak at 4.60% and cuts would begin in May 2027.

Not all bank savings growing as interest rates rise
If you missed it, business reporter Adelaide Miller looked at savings rates and whether higher rates are flowing through to customers.

Savers with billions of dollars in Australian banks could be missing out on the benefits of the rising cash rate as a result of onerous account conditions or because they have not opted for the right savings product.

While the major banks quickly increased the interest paid on mortgages after the September rate hike, customers with high-interest savings accounts have not been finding the corresponding interest rate increases as lucrative.
Canstar said the rate increases were applied only to a select few of the banks' savings account products and came with strict conditions.
Unless savers meet those requirements, they revert to a base interest rate that the banks have kept flat at 0.10 per cent.
Key Event
Consumer confidence at a five-month low
Ahead of today's rates decision, ANZ-Roy Morgan Australian Consumer Confidence and inflation expectations have dropped to a five-month low.
According to the research released this morning, consumer confidence fell 1.7pts last week to 66.2pts, the lowest level since late May.
ANZ economist Sophia Angala says the fall was led by weaker conditions in personal finance.

"On a four-week moving average basis, the inflation expectations figure remains at its highest level since late May," she says."This follows last week’s Q3 CPI print, which showed annual trimmed mean (underlying) inflation was slightly stronger than expected at 3.7% y/y."
"On a four-week moving average basis, the inflation expectations figure remains at its highest level since late May," she says.
"This follows last week’s Q3 CPI print, which showed annual trimmed mean (underlying) inflation was slightly stronger than expected at 3.7% y/y."
She says consumer confidence remains well below its long-run average and expects the RBA to raise the cash rate by 25bp today, with some risk the cash rate reaches 5.10% in December or February.
Key Event
Shares of AMP, coal and oil companies among today's worst-performing ASX stocks
We're two hours into the trading day, and the Australian share market has erased most of its early gains.
The ASX 200 had risen by 0.2% to 8,872 points.
Some of the stocks weighing on the broader market are in the energy and financial sectors.
Shares of AMP have fallen 7.7%, making it the worst performer on Australia's main stock index.

Other companies on this "weakest performers" list include coal miners Yancoal, New Hope and Whitehaven Coal, along with oil and gas companies such as Woodside Energy and Viva Energy, all down between 3% and 5.5%.

Prior to this, they were actively encouraging young people to enter the property market with deposits as little as 5%. I committed my life savings to buying a home, and have watched the value of those savings wiped out on paper in 6 months. Young, middle-class Australians (often with young families like me) who have worked hard, saved diligently and taken on enormous financial commitments are continuously slogged with high income taxes and rate increases, with apparently little thought or care from the RBA or the government. It's hard not to feel despondent and angry.

Key Event
David Jones' lender 'remains supportive', despite concerns about retailer's ongoing survival
The ailing department store chain David Jones has reportedly missed a deadline to file its 2026 accounts with corporate regulator ASIC and plans to close up to 26 stores.
Speculation in the financial press is that the 188-year-old retail chain — with its significant debts, declining sales and struggles to pay suppliers — may not survive much longer.
David Jones previously secured a lifeline from British financial firm Hilco Capital, which provided the retailer with a $230 million loan.
In a statement, Hilco said it "has funded above the agreed facility to allow David Jones to increase stock holdings ahead of the busy Christmas trade and sales period".
"Hilco remains supportive of the business, and any inference otherwise is false."

Key Event
Qantas and Virgin shares surge on plunging oil price
Apart from gold miners, airline companies are also doing well on the ASX today.
Virgin Australia's shares have soared 7.1% to $2.66, while Qantas's have jumped 6% to $9.33.
The 8% drop in oil prices overnight is good news for businesses that consume extraordinary amounts of fuel, like airlines.
Jet fuel prices have more than doubled since the US and Israel waged war against Iran in late February.

Virgin, Qantas and Qantas's lower-cost subsidiary Jetstar have tried to reduce the impact of these higher fuel prices by raising airfares and suspending several routes, particularly in regional areas, that are not particularly profitable.
Key Event
ASX gold miners surge after rebound in precious metal's price
Several of today's best performers on the ASX are gold stocks.
That's after the price of gold rebounded from its one-year low overnight.
The spot price of the precious metal jumped 2% overnight to about $US3,946 per ounce. So it's still below the $US4,000 mark.
It was the sharp fall in oil prices (-8%) that contributed to the recovery in gold.

Markets are increasingly convinced that Donald Trump will not order strikes against Iran when the US midterm elections are over, and that the US and Iran will take steps to negotiate and end their war. Though we've seen this story play out many times before.
Much lower oil prices generally lead to inflation falling, eventually, and potentially fewer interest rate hikes being "priced in" by money markets.
So that's the gist of why gold prices and Australian gold miners are doing well today.
Broad gains at start of trade on ASX
Twenty minutes into the session, the gains are fairly broad-based.

Key Event
RBA forecast to raise interest rates at 2:30pm AEDT
The Reserve Bank board will deliver its November interest rate decision at 2:30pm AEDT.
At the same time, the central bank's updated economic forecasts will be released in its quarterly Statement on Monetary Policy.
NAB isn't certain this will be the last rate hike
NAB is one of the major banks forecasting that the Reserve Bank of Australia will raise the cash rate for the fifth time this year, taking it to 4.85%.
So will this be the monetary board's last rate hike for a while? NAB's chief economist, Sally Auld, doesn't seem so sure.
Here's what she just told the ABC News Channel.
"As things stand today, we are forecasting a rate hike this afternoon. That is the last one we have in our forecast.
"We need to be open to the possibility, given the shift in rhetoric from the Reserve Bank, that it is possible we might see more interest rate rises in the next few months.
"We will take time to digest what we see today and think about the outlook but we are in for a period of reasonably elevated rates for a while yet."
Key Event
Four rate hikes still filtering through
The Reserve Bank is widely tipped to increase the cash rate today for the fifth time this year, taking it to its highest level in 18 years, at 4.85%.
NAB's chief economist, Sally Auld, is not dissenting from the consensus, telling ABC's News Channel that it would be "a big surprise" if the monetary board didn't vote to hike.
She also noted that the full effect of the previous rate hikes was still filtering through the Australian economy.
"The Reserve Bank will say the full impact of a rate hike usually takes 12–18 months to be fully seen in the economy and data.
"We started in February. The last one was only in September. We are not at the point where we can see the full impact.
"We have seen a slowing in the economy and we see that in our NAB survey, business confidence and conditions are running below long-term averages.
"It feels like the economy is adjusting to higher interest rates but we're not at the end of the story and that story will be with us for some time in the year ahead."
Big tech companies reporting in the US
Anthropic and Apple are just two of the major US tech companies that released their results overnight.

Apple's sales results beat Wall Street expectations, driven by early demand for its iPhone 18 Pro lineup. It has also increased prices on some products, such as the iPhone 17, to offset higher chip costs.
Meanwhile, Anthropic released results showing revenue growth slowed sharply in the third quarter. The AI startup is also flagging new risks ahead of its blockbuster IPO.
Overall, the tech index Nasdaq lost 1%. Here's some analysis from Capital's Kyle Rodda on why:

Fears persist about the outlook for the so-called AI trade, with the stocks of companies across the AI supply chain tumbling on comparatively underwhelming earnings growth and a possible peak in the investment boom.
The dynamic dragged the NASDAQ into technical correction territory, with a week ahead full of interest rate uncertainty and US political risk only adding to the drawdown.
Although it’s not technically an AI play, Apple’s quarterly results released after the bell look as though at the margins they will weigh on market sentiment.
While beating on the top line because of strong iPhone sales, a miss in China revenues appears to be responsible for a drop in the stock in after-hours trade.

The other ways to offer mortgages

Would long-term fixed-rate home loans, like the 30-year mortgages common in the US, help Australian households manage the impact of RBA rate changes by giving them certainty over their repayments, and why aren't they widely offered here? At the same time, what drawbacks might they carry, such as higher costs for borrowers, greater interest rate risk for lenders, or a weaker transmission of monetary policy that could make inflation harder for the RBA to control?

Key Event
Average borrower faces $456 increase in 2026: Canstar
Financial comparison site Canstar has crunched some numbers ahead of today's RBA decision, which is expected to see the cash rate rise to 4.85%, an 18-year high.
"Australia may be revisiting 2008-era interest rates, but today's borrowers have far bigger mortgages to contend with," Canstar said.

It calculated that the average new owner-occupier loan has nearly tripled since then, from $254,000 in November 2008 to $731,000 today, an increase of 188%, while the median property price has risen by 129%, with it now sitting at $884,855.
Canstar says a 0.25% cash rate hike this afternoon would bring the cumulative increase in monthly minimum home loan repayments since February to $456 for a borrower with a $600,000 loan.

The most recent inflation data came in slightly hotter than had been forecast, and followed several senior RBA officials talking up the need for the board to do more in order to bring inflation down.
That shifted market sentiment and economist forecasts firmly in favour of an 0.25 percentage point hike to the cash rate — with will flow through to mortgage borrowers and savers.

Analysis: Look to deficits, not government spending
Good morning! Jumping in to share this piece from our chief business correspondent Ian Verrender. As usual, his Tuesday morning analysis is required reading:
Take a deep breath.
It'll only take a few minutes from Michele Bullock's ascension to the podium at this afternoon's post rate decision press conference for the blame game to begin.
Who is responsible for the inflation outbreak?
She won't answer, at least directly. And she certainly won't deliver the answer required by a baying press pack.
For most of this year the opposition has cleverly sheeted responsibility home to the federal government with accusations of profligate spending.
It's not just gaining traction, it's become an article of fact.
Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson is having a field day.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers, it is said, is out of control, spending your hard-earned tax dollars like a drunken sailor, pushing up the price of almost everything and forcing the Reserve Bank to counter with rate hikes.
It's simple and it's neat, the kind of messaging that resonates with an electorate tired of being whacked around the ears, first by runaway prices and then by higher mortgage repayments.
There's just one problem. It's hugely misleading on a number of fronts.

Key Event
Unemployment rate to push over 5 per cent: CBA
CBA analysts also reiterated gloomier forecasts for Australia's economy in their morning note today.
It comes ahead of a widely tipped rate increase by the Reserve Bank of Australia to tackle rising inflation.
Assuming the RBA hikes today, it would be the fifth hike this year and the highest cash rate target in 18 years at 4.85%.

A 125bp tightening is material in an economy with high household debt. Our Australian economics team now expect economic growth to fall to 1.0%/yr by mid‑2027, compared to our previous forecast of 1.8%/yr.
The unemployment rate is now forecast to increase to 5.1% compared to our previous peak of 4.8%.
CBA predicts a 'sell the fact' with AUD
The local currency dropped a touch below US 70 cents overnight, ahead of today's rates decision by the Reserve Bank of Australia at 2:30pm AEDT.
Commonwealth Bank's economists have just put out their morning note about currencies and what the AUD could do.
A 25bp hike is widely expected by Australian economists and market participants, including ourselves. With a 25bp hike around 80% priced, the upside to AUD/USD is limited in our view.
The post‑meeting statement or the press conference would have to be very hawkish to push AUD/USD through resistance at 0.7076 (76.4% fibbo) in our view.
By contrast, we would not be surprised to see a ‘buy the rumour, sell the fact’ reaction where AUD/USD falls after the hike because the hike has been well telegraphed by RBA officials.
Oil prices dive more than 7 per cent
There's been a big move in oil markets overnight, reportedly on comments by US President Donald Trump and on talks between Iranian and Qatari officials.
Brent crude futures settled $US8.66, or 7.63%, lower to $US104.77 a barrel. US West Texas Intermediate crude was down $US7.66, or 7.36%, at $US96.46.
Brent had ended October at its highest level in six months on concerns that the Middle East conflict could escalate again after Tuesday's US midterm elections.
Yet Trump on Monday said that Iran wanted to make a deal to end the war and that such an agreement "could happen."
On Monday evening, Qatari mediators travelled to Tehran for talks with Iran's Foreign Minister on a potential US-Iran deal.
While these signs of progress pushed oil prices lower, one analyst, Pavel Molchanov, told Reuters that scepticism is warranted after many "false dawns” in recent months.
